interviewQuestions.question: Would you build this yourself or use a managed service?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by asking whether this component is core to what actually differentiates this product, or commodity infrastructure that any competitor would also need. For commodity pieces — a message queue, a search index, an object store — I'd buy: a 15-person team building its own queue for "full control" is really signing up for ongoing patching, scaling, and on-call on top of the build cost, which pulls time straight from the actual product.

I'd build only where the component is the differentiation itself — a company whose entire value is search relevance building its own ranking system, for example, because that logic *is* the product.

I'd name the trade-off explicitly: buying costs long-term flexibility and unit economics at scale in exchange for speed and lower operational burden now, which is why some companies later migrate from bought to built — not because buying was wrong initially, but because the calculus changed with scale.

**Testing:** whether you evaluate build-vs-buy against this specific component's differentiation and true operational cost, rather than a reflexive default.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Build vs. managed service for this component

interviewQuestions.question: Your team already built something in-house that a managed service now does just as well — do you migrate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat this the same way I'd evaluate a build-vs-buy call for a brand-new component, just with switching costs added to one side of the ledger. First, is the in-house version core to differentiation, or did we build it back when no good managed option existed and it's really commodity infrastructure now? If it's the latter, the managed service's ongoing lower operational burden is the argument for migrating — the fact that we already built it isn't a reason to keep operating it forever.

I'd weigh the migration cost explicitly against the ongoing cost of continuing to operate the in-house version — patching, on-call, the engineers who understand it and could be doing something else — and prefer a phased migration over a risky big-bang cutover.

Sunk cost is the trap here: having already paid to build something isn't a reason to keep paying to operate it if a managed alternative is now clearly cheaper on an ongoing basis.

**Testing:** whether you can revisit an existing build decision on its current merits instead of anchoring to the fact that it was already built.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Migrating an existing in-house system to managed

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide when a managed service's missing feature is a real dealbreaker versus something you can work around?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd check two things: is the missing feature tied to what's actually core to our differentiation, or is it a gap in otherwise-commodity infrastructure? And is there a genuine workaround — even an inelegant one — or is the gap a hard, structural blocker?

A missing feature on commodity infrastructure with a workaround available almost never justifies building a replacement — the operational cost of owning that whole category of infrastructure vastly outweighs one awkward workaround. A hard blocker on something that's actually core to the product tips the other way, since it means the managed option can't support the thing we're actually trying to be best at.

Concretely: a managed search product missing a minor ranking tweak for a non-core feature, I'd work around; a managed search product structurally unable to support the ranking approach that *is* our product, I'd treat as a real signal to build.

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish a genuine architectural blocker from an inconvenience you're tempted to over-react to.
